lead: A Turing machine does not only say yes or no. It can also write an answer on its tape. A function is computable when some machine halts on every input and leaves the correct output. Allow the machine to loop on some inputs, and the function is partial computable. This idea turns yes/no questions into arithmetic: a language L is decidable exactly when its characteristic function, 1 on L and 0 outside, is computable. Compilers, solvers and calculators all compute functions, so the line between computable and not matters.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for decidable versus r.e., 6.3 for the halting problem, and Unit 5 for the machine model.

blocks.text: Fix an alphabet Σ. Σ* is the set of all finite strings over Σ. A function f: Σ* → Σ* maps strings to strings. A Turing machine M computes f when M, started with x on its tape, halts with f(x) written on the tape. Then f is computable, also called total computable or Turing-computable.
A partial function f: Σ* ⇀ Σ* may be undefined on some inputs. It is partial computable when some machine halts with f(x) on every input where f is defined, and loops forever where f is undefined.

Every total computable function is partial computable. The converse fails: a partial function may have no value at some input, and no machine can halt and print a value that does not exist. Totality is the promise that matters. A compiler that sometimes loops forever is not a total function from source code to object code.
f is computable ⟺ some TM halts on every x ∈ Σ* with f(x) on its tape
blocks.where: Σ* is the set of all strings over Σ.

blocks.text: For a partial f, the machine must halt with f(x) where f is defined and may loop where f is undefined.

Every Turing machine is a finite object: finitely many states, a finite tape alphabet, a finite transition table. Write each item in binary and join the items with a fixed separator. The result is ⟨M⟩, the encoding of M. Likewise ⟨M,w⟩ encodes a machine together with an input string w.

A pairing function packs two numbers into one. One bijection is pair(i,j) = 2ⁱ(2j+1) − 1. Gödel numbering encodes a sequence n₁,…,n_k as a single number, for example 2<sup>n₁</sup>·3<sup>n₂</sup>⋯p<sub>k</sub><sup>n_k</sup> using the first k primes p₁=2, p₂=3, …, and each exponent is the corresponding n<sub>i</sub>. Grammars are finite too: list the productions and encode the list.

Encodings must be computable and decodable: a machine can read ⟨M⟩ and rebuild M's table. Once machines are strings, they can be listed M₁, M₂, M₃, … and handed to other machines. That is what the universal machine does (Unit 5), and it is why the halting problem can be stated at all (see 6.3).

sections.h3: Characteristic function and the decidability test

blocks.text: For a language L over Σ, the characteristic function χ_L: Σ* → {0,1} answers the membership question as a number.
χ_L(x) = 1 if x ∈ L, and 0 if x ∉ L
blocks.where: L is a language over Σ; χ_L is always total when written this way.

blocks.text: Theorem. L is decidable if and only if χ_L is computable.
Proof (⇒). Let D decide L, halting on every x. Build M: run D on x, write 1 if D accepts, write 0 if D rejects, halt. M halts on every input, so χ_L is total computable.
Proof (⇐). Let M compute χ_L. Build D: run M on x, accept when the output is 1, reject when it is 0. Since M halts on every input, D decides L.

The r.e. case replaces total by partial. L is r.e. if and only if L is the domain of a partial computable function, that is, L = {x : ψ(x) is defined}. If A accepts L, set ψ(x) = 1 when A halts on x, undefined otherwise; the domain is L. Conversely, if M computes ψ, run M and accept whenever it halts; the accepted set is the domain.
Equivalently, a nonempty L is r.e. if and only if L is the range of a total computable function. Run the recogniser on the strings in dovetail order and print each string it accepts.

sections.h3: Composition and the hierarchy of functions

blocks.text: Composition. If f and g are computable, so is h(x) = g(f(x)): run the machine for f, feed its output to the machine for g. The same proof works for partial functions, with h(x) defined exactly when both stages halt.

Strictness. The total computable functions are a strict subset of the partial computable ones. Define g(M,w) = 1 when M halts on w, undefined otherwise. A simulator computes g, so g is partial computable. If g were total computable, halting would be decidable; it is not (see 6.3).
Counting. There are countably many Turing machines and uncountably many functions Σ* → Σ*. So almost every function is not computable by any machine.

Recursive function theory builds the same class from zero, successor and projections, closed under composition, primitive recursion and μ-recursion (minimisation). The names are enough here; the resulting class equals the partial computable functions.

spec.aria: Three tape rows: aaa with the head on cell 1; the head on the blank cell 4 after three moves; aaaa after the head writes a there and halts.

examples.question: A unary number n is written as the string aⁿ. (a) Show that f(n) = n + 1 is computable, tracing the machine on the input aaa. (b) Define g(M,w) = 1 when M halts on w, undefined otherwise, and state exactly how much of g is computable.
steps: Encode: aaa holds three a's, so n = 3.
Machine M: move the head right while the cell holds a; at the first blank cell write a; halt.
Trace: cells 1, 2, 3 hold a and cell 4 is blank. The head steps right three times, writes a in cell 4, and halts with aaaa.
So f(aaa) = aaaa, that is, 3 maps to 4. The same moves work for every n and M always halts, so f is total computable.
For g: simulate M on w step by step. If the simulation stops, write 1 and halt. If M never stops, the simulation never stops. So g is partial computable.
If g were total computable, a machine would halt on every ⟨M,w⟩ and print 1 when M halts on w and 0 otherwise, which decides halting. Halting is undecidable, so g is not total computable.
examples.answer: f is total computable, with f(aaa) = aaaa (3 → 4); g is partial computable but not total computable.

traps: Assuming every r.e. language has a computable characteristic function; only the decidable ones do, and for the rest χ_L is a total function that no machine computes. The partial computable object is the semi-characteristic function: 1 on L, undefined outside L.
Treating a partial function as if it had a value at every input; writing f(x) for x outside the domain is meaningless.
Confusing 'partial computable' with 'not computable'. A partial computable function is computed by a machine; it simply need not halt everywhere.
Thinking a machine that loops on some inputs still decides its language. A decider must halt on every input and print 0 or 1.
Mixing domain and range. L r.e. means L is the domain of a partial computable function; as a range you need the empty-set exception.

quiz.q: Define a computable function f: Σ* → Σ*.
quiz.a: Some Turing machine halts on every x ∈ Σ* with f(x) written on its tape.

quiz.q: Why is every total computable function partial computable, while the converse fails?
quiz.a: A total function never uses the loop option, so the same machine meets the partial definition. A partial function may be undefined somewhere, so no always-halting machine can compute it as a total function.

quiz.q: Let L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}. Give χ_L(aabb) and χ_L(abab).
quiz.a: aabb ∈ L, so χ_L(aabb) = 1. abab ∉ L, so χ_L(abab) = 0.

quiz.q: On unary strings, f(x) = x+1 and g(x) = x+x. Compute h = g∘f on aaa.
quiz.a: f(aaa) = aaaa, length 4. g(aaaa) = aaaaaaaa, length 8. So h(aaa) = aaaaaaaa.

quiz.q: Explain why the halting function g is not total computable.
quiz.a: A total machine for g would, on ⟨M,w⟩, halt with 1 or with 0, deciding halting. The halting problem is undecidable, so no such total machine exists. g is still partial computable by simulation.

quiz.q: What is ⟨M,w⟩ and why is an encoding needed?
quiz.a: ⟨M,w⟩ is a string encoding a machine M and an input w. Encoding lets one machine take another machine as data, which the universal machine and the halting problem both require.

quiz.q: Use a counting argument to show that some functions Σ* → Σ* are not computable.
quiz.a: Turing machines have finitely many descriptions, so there are countably many of them. The set of all functions Σ* → Σ* is uncountable. Each machine computes at most one function, so uncountably many functions have no machine.

beyond: Not for the exam. Recursive function theory, also called computability theory, is a full subject: Kleene's normal form theorem, the recursion theorem and the arithmetical hierarchy all grow from these definitions. Proof assistants such as Coq and Lean formalise computability so that every function they define is total and checkable. Algorithmic information theory measures a string by the length of the shortest program that prints it. Search for 'primitive recursive functions', 'μ-recursion' and 'Kleene's T predicate' to go further.
